lesson.subtitle: Lesson 8 -- The Podcast Habit
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Cauê de França | Lesson 8 -- The Podcast Habit
lesson.grammar_point: used to / would for past habits x be used to / get used to (+ noun or -ing) for what is normal or is becoming normal

listenings.text: I've been hosting this show for six years, and I've learned a lot from my listeners. Most of them tune in on the go. In the car, on the train, at the gym. Almost nobody sits down at home just to listen. When I started, I used to think that longer was better. My first episodes were nearly an hour. Then the messages started coming in. People said, I love the show, but I never finish an episode. So I changed. Now the episodes are bite-sized, fifteen minutes or less. And guess what? More people listen to the end. They told me shorter episodes were easier to stick to. They were right.

I work nights at a hospital, so my commute is at seven in the morning, when everybody else is going to work. I used to sleep on the bus, or at least try to. It never really worked. Then a colleague told me about a podcast about history. I tried it, and now I'm completely used to it. Bus, headphones, an episode. It helps me switch off after the shift. At first it was hard to get used to the speed of the hosts and their accents. One is Scottish, one is American. But after a few weeks I stopped noticing. Now, if I forget my headphones, the trip feels twice as long.

Streaks work. You do something every day, the number grows, and after a while you just don't want to lose it. That's why language apps use them. But there's a problem. When people break a long streak, they often give up completely. They think, well, it's gone, why bother? So I teach my clients a simple rule. You can miss one day. Life happens. But never two days in a row. If you fall behind on Monday, Tuesday is not optional. Consistency isn't about being perfect. It's about getting back on track, fast. Most people get used to the rule in about a month, and it changes everything.

reading.rtitle: Twenty Minutes on the Train: How a Habit Is Born
paras: Two years ago, Marina used to spend her commute scrolling the news on her phone. Every morning she would read the same headlines three times and arrive at work tense and tired. She wanted to improve her English, but she was not used to listening to it for more than a few minutes. Real English felt too fast, and the hosts of the podcasts she tried seemed to speak in a hurry.

Her solution was small. She subscribed to one podcast with bite-sized episodes, about ten minutes long, and attached it to a habit she already had: the train. No train, no podcast; train, podcast. It sounds simple, and it is. Experts on habits often say that consistency matters more than intensity: ten minutes every day is better than two hours once a month. During the first weeks, Marina found it hard to get used to the speed of the hosts, but she stuck to it.

She also kept a streak, like the ones on language apps. Some weeks she fell behind, and her streak went back to zero. Instead of giving up, she started again the next day. Today she is used to listening on the go, and she tunes in to three different shows. She still reads the news, but now she makes time for it at lunch. The train belongs to English.
